compatibility.title: Which BMW Group Models Use the N74B66?
compatibility.intro: The N74B66 is BMW Group's flagship V12, introduced in the Rolls‑Royce Ghost in 2010 and later appearing in the BMW M760Li xDrive - the last V12‑powered BMW production car. The engine is also fitted to the Wraith and Dawn coupe/convertible models. All N74B66 applications are flagship luxury models with six‑figure price points when new.

costGuide.title: BMW N74B66 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an N74B66 typically takes 20-28 hours at £100-£150/hr (independent V12 specialist) - the 60‑degree V12's complex packaging, twin turbochargers and intricate cooling system make this BMW's most labour‑intensive engine swap.
paragraphs: The biggest price movers for an N74B66 replacement are turbocharger condition (OEM replacements are £3,000+ each), whether the valve stem seals have been addressed, and the state of the VANOS and Valvetronic systems. The TU variant (M760Li xDrive) features xDrive‑specific oil pan and sump design, which adds complexity and cost. Engines with documented cooling system history and regular oil changes command a premium. See our full /prices/reconditioned-engine-cost guide for more detail.

failures.title: BMW N74B66 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Valve Stem Seal Degradation - oil consumption across the N74 family
items.whatHappens: Like many BMW V8 and V12 engines, the N74B66's valve stem seals degrade over time, allowing oil to pass into the combustion chamber. This results in blue smoke on startup (particularly after idling), increased oil consumption, and fouled spark plugs. The V12's high operating temperatures accelerate seal wear.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a significant job - the cylinder heads must be accessed, typically costing £2,500-£5,000 at a specialist. If caught early, the engine can be saved; if ignored, oil consumption can lead to catalytic converter failure and turbocharger damage. → Read our full /failures/valve-stem-seal-failure guide

items.title: Turbocharger Oil Line Coking and Turbocharger Failure
items.whatHappens: The N74B66's twin turbochargers are fed by oil lines that can become coked (carbon‑blocked) over time, particularly if the engine is frequently idled or subjected to short journeys. Coked oil lines restrict oil flow to the turbochargers, leading to bearing failure. Symptoms include reduced power, unusual noises from the turbo area, and in severe cases, complete turbocharger failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbocharger replacement is a specialist job (£3,000-£5,000 per turbo). If failure has occurred due to coking, the oil lines must also be replaced or cleaned to prevent recurrence. Regular oil changes with BMW LL‑01 approved oil are critical.

items.title: Double VANOS System Wear
items.whatHappens: The N74B66's Double VANOS variable valve timing system is subjected to significant stress, particularly on higher‑mileage examples. VANOS wear can cause poor low‑end torque, hesitation on acceleration, and a characteristic "splat" noise from the VANOS units on startup.
items.repairVsReplace: VANOS seal replacement is a specialist job (£1,500-£3,000). If the VANOS units have failed, replacement is required. Often addressed when valve stem seals are being replaced as part of a comprehensive engine overhaul.

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch
items.whatHappens: The N74B66's timing chains can stretch over time, particularly if oil changes have been neglected. Symptoms include a rattle on cold start from the timing chain area, and in severe cases, chain slip causing valve and piston damage.
items.repairVsReplace: Timing chain replacement is a major job (£2,000-£4,000) requiring engine disassembly. If the chain has slipped, replacement is the only safe option - valve damage is almost certain.

items.title: Cooling System Weaknesses - water pump, thermostat and hoses
items.whatHappens: The N74B66 generates immense heat and has a complex cooling system with multiple radiators, an electric water pump and numerous hoses. Weak points include the water pump, thermostat housing and plastic coolant pipes that become brittle with age. Coolant loss is the most common early warning - ignored, it leads to overheating and catastrophic engine damage.
items.repairVsReplace: Water pump and thermostat replacement is a significant job (£800-£1,800) due to the tight engine bay. If the engine has overheated, head gasket failure may justify a full replacement.

failures.goodYearsLine: The N74B66 was introduced in 2010. The N74B66TU (Technical Update) variant was developed specifically for the G11/G12 M760Li xDrive from 2016, featuring revised cooling, different turbocharger mapping and xDrive‑specific oil pan and sump design. The TU variant also benefits from improvements to the oil separation system and VANOS components. The N74B66 is significantly more reliable than the naturally aspirated N73 it replaced, and has proven capable of 100,000+ trouble‑free miles with diligent maintenance.

variants.title: N74B66 Sub‑Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The N74B66 family covers several variants, from the original Rolls‑Royce Ghost engine to the BMW M760Li xDrive Technical Update. Understanding which variant you have is essential when sourcing a replacement - the TU variant in particular has specific components for xDrive applications that are not interchangeable with Rolls‑Royce‑spec engines. - Fitted to: Rolls‑Royce Ghost (2010-present), Rolls‑Royce Ghost Extended - Key technical difference: Tuned for effortless torque delivery rather than outright power. Produces 563 hp (420 kW) and 779 Nm torque. Focused on refinement and near‑silent operation. Uses a 10.25:1 compression ratio and specific ECU calibration for Ghost's "pinnacle of luxury" character. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above - valve stem seal degradation, turbocharger oil line coking and VANOS wear. Ghost‑spec engines are typically low‑mileage but may suffer from carbon buildup due to frequent idling. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with the M760Li xDrive TU variant - the Ghost uses a different ECU calibration, oil pan design (not xDrive‑specific) and cooling system. Fitting a TU engine into a Ghost requires extensive ECU and cooling system changes. - Fitted to: Rolls‑Royce Wraith (2013-present), Rolls‑Royce Wraith Black Badge - Key technical difference: The most powerful N74B66 variant in Rolls‑Royce form. Produces 624 hp (465 kW) and 800 Nm torque. Features a more aggressive tune than the Ghost, reflecting the Wraith's grand touring character. Higher boost levels and revised ECU calibration. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern. Wraith‑spec engines are subject to higher stress than Ghost‑spec due to the power increase. Regular oil changes are critical. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with any other N74B66 variant - the ECU calibration is unique to the Wraith. Fitting a Wraith engine into a Ghost would require ECU modifications. - Fitted to: Rolls‑Royce Dawn (2016-present), Rolls‑Royce Dawn Black Badge - Key technical difference: Same power output as the Ghost (563 hp) but with specific cooling modifications for the open‑top body style. The Dawn's convertibility requires additional cooling capacity to handle the reduced airflow when the roof is down. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern. Dawn‑spec engines may be subject to additional stress due to the convertible body's cooling requirements. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with Ghost‑spec engines - the cooling system is different. Fitting a Ghost engine into a Dawn would require cooling system modifications. - Fitted to: BMW 7 Series G11/G12 M760Li xDrive (2016-2022) - Key technical difference: Technical Update variant developed specifically for the M760Li xDrive. Features revised cooling system components, different turbocharger mapping, and an xDrive‑specific oil pan and sump design to accommodate the all‑wheel‑drive system. Produces 585-610 hp depending on the specific TU iteration. The last V12 offered in a BMW‑badged production car. - Sub‑code‑specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern but benefits from improvements to the oil separation system and VANOS components. The xDrive‑specific oil pan adds complexity to oil change and maintenance procedures. - Interchange note: Not a direct swap with any Rolls‑Royce‑spec variant - the TU engine has different oil pan, cooling system and ECU calibration. Fitting a non‑xDrive engine into an M760Li would require significant modification.

relatives.description: the 6.0‑litre (5,972 cc) V12 that preceded the N74B66, fitted to the F01/F02 760Li from 2009-2015. It featured the same 89mm bore but a shorter 80mm stroke, producing 544 hp and 750 Nm. The N74B66 expanded displacement to 6.6 litres by increasing stroke to 88.3mm, delivering more torque and refinement. The N74B60 is less common and has similar maintenance considerations.

With further bore/stroke increases and improved emissions, it represents the final evolution of BMW's V12 before the N74 family was retired from BMW production in 2022. Not fitted to any BMW‑badged model.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement N74B66 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used N74B66 can be a cost‑effective option for high‑mileage examples, but only if the engine comes from a low‑mileage, well‑documented donor with proof of regular oil changes and cooling system maintenance. Given the engine's known weaknesses (valve stem seals, turbocharger oil lines, VANOS), a used unit without history is a high‑risk purchase - the cost of addressing these issues can quickly exceed the purchase price. Used prices from £10,500-£15,000 reflect this risk. Link once:

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A properly reconditioned N74B66 is the recommended choice for most M760Li and Rolls‑Royce owners. A full recon should address the engine's known weak points: new valve stem seals (upgraded materials), turbocharger inspection and oil line replacement, new water pump and thermostat, full gasket set, VANOS rebuild, and cooling system overhaul. Given the £14,622-£21,609 supply cost and the host vehicle value (£25,000-£100,000+ for a well‑maintained example), this is the best balance of cost and reliability. A 12-24 month warranty is essential on an engine of this complexity. Link once:

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full N74B66 rebuild is justified for low‑mileage, concours‑condition examples or where the owner plans long‑term preservation. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, and strengthened turbocharger oil lines. Rebuild costs (£18,000-£25,000+) are significant - only consider this for high‑value, collector‑grade examples. Link once:

For Rolls‑Royce examples, the higher retained value comfortably absorbs the replacement cost. The honest marketplace‑neutrality position is: if your N74B66 has suffered catastrophic failure and your M760Li is worth under £25,000, evaluate scrap or part‑exchange value before committing.

items.question: What are the most common failures on the BMW N74B66?
items.answer: The N74B66's main problems are associated with rapid coking at idle, turbocharger failure up to 100,000 km due to coking in oil lines, Double VANOS system wear by 150,000 km, timing chain stretch after 150,000 km, and valve stem seal degradation causing lubricant consumption. Cooling system problems with the water pump and thermostat are also common. Oil leaks can be a concern, and high‑pressure fuel pump failure is reported on some examples. → Read our full V12 engine failure guide for more detail.
bullets: Carbon buildup from direct injection is a significant issue on high‑mileage examples.
Turbocharger failure is often caused by oil line coking - preventative oil changes are critical.
Timing chain replacement is expensive and requires engine removal.

items.question: Which BMW and Rolls‑Royce models use the N74B66 engine?
items.answer: The N74B66 is fitted to the Rolls‑Royce Ghost (2010-present), Rolls‑Royce Wraith (2013-present), and Rolls‑Royce Dawn (2016-present). In BMW‑badged form, the N74B66TU is fitted to the G11/G12 BMW 7 Series M760Li xDrive from 2016 to 2022. The engine was not carried over to the G70 7 Series, which means BMW's V12 era ended in 2022. → Enter your registration to confirm your exact N74 variant.

Check your V5C or engine block stamp to confirm which N74 variant you have.

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt N74B66?
items.answer: For most N74B66 owners, a reconditioned unit with new valve stem seals, timing chains, turbocharger oil lines and full cooling system overhaul is the recommended choice - it addresses the engine's key weaknesses and comes with a 12-24 month warranty. Used units are cheaper but carry high risk without full documentation, particularly regarding turbocharger and VANOS condition. Rebuilds are justified for low‑mileage, high‑value examples (M760Li, Ghost) or where the owner plans long‑term preservation. → Compare all three options from vetted V12 specialists.

Reconditioned: best balance - all common weak points addressed, warranty included.
Rebuilt: ideal for collector‑grade examples or long‑term keepers.

items.question: What is the difference between the N74B66 and the N74B66TU?
items.answer: The N74B66TU (Technical Update) is the version fitted to the BMW G11/G12 M760Li xDrive from 2016. It features revised cooling system components, different turbocharger mapping, and an xDrive‑specific oil pan and sump design to accommodate the all‑wheel‑drive system. Power output is 585-610 hp compared to 563-624 hp across the broader N74B66 family. The TU variant also benefits from improvements to the oil separation system and VANOS components. → Verify your N74B66 variant now.
bullets: M760Li xDrive has the TU variant - it's not just a calibration difference.
TU engines are not a direct swap into Rolls‑Royce applications without ECU and cooling changes.

items.question: Is the N74B66 reliable, and what mileage can I expect?
items.answer: The N74B66 is one of BMW's most robust V12 designs, with an estimated lifespan of approximately 320,000 km (200,000 miles) when properly maintained. Many Rolls‑Royce and M760Li owners report 100,000+ trouble‑free miles with diligent maintenance. However, the engine is complex and expensive to maintain - turbocharger oil line coking, valve stem seal degradation and VANOS wear are real considerations on higher‑mileage examples. → Find a specialist who knows the N74 V12 inside out.
bullets: Budget for turbocharger oil line inspection and cleaning around 60,000 miles.
Valve stem seal replacement should be considered around 80,000-100,000 miles.
Full service history is essential - this is not an engine to neglect.
The N74B66 is significantly more reliable than the naturally aspirated N73 it replaced.

mainEntity.name: How much does a BMW N74B66 engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement N74B66 engine typically costs between £14,622 and £21,609 depending on condition and specification [THIRD‑PARTY]. Used units in good condition average around £14,622, while new or professionally reconditioned engines can reach £21,609. Fitting costs add significantly - the V12's complex packaging and 60‑degree bank angle make this one of BMW's most labour‑intensive engine swaps, with specialist labour rates of £100-£150/hr and installation times exceeding 25 hours. Supply‑only excludes fitting. Prices vary significantly by variant - TU versions for M760Li command a premium. Rolls‑Royce‑spec engines may have different part numbers and calibration. Always compare quotes from V12‑specialist workshops.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common failures on the BMW N74B66?

acceptedAnswer.text: The N74B66's main problems are associated with rapid coking at idle, turbocharger failure up to 100,000 km due to coking in oil lines, Double VANOS system wear by 150,000 km, timing chain stretch after 150,000 km, and valve stem seal degradation causing lubricant consumption. Cooling system problems with the water pump and thermostat are also common. Oil leaks can be a concern, and high‑pressure fuel pump failure is reported on some examples. Carbon buildup from direct injection is a significant issue on high‑mileage examples. Turbocharger failure is often caused by oil line coking - preventative oil changes are critical. Timing chain replacement is expensive and requires engine removal.

mainEntity.name: Which BMW and Rolls‑Royce models use the N74B66 engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: The N74B66 is fitted to the Rolls‑Royce Ghost (2010-present), Rolls‑Royce Wraith (2013-present), and Rolls‑Royce Dawn (2016-present). In BMW‑badged form, the N74B66TU is fitted to the G11/G12 BMW 7 Series M760Li xDrive from 2016 to 2022. The engine was not carried over to the G70 7 Series, which means BMW's V12 era ended in 2022. All N74B66 applications are flagship luxury models. Check your V5C or engine block stamp to confirm which N74 variant you have. Rolls‑Royce‑spec engines are tuned differently from BMW M760Li versions.

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or rebuilt N74B66?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most N74B66 owners, a reconditioned unit with new valve stem seals, timing chains, turbocharger oil lines and full cooling system overhaul is the recommended choice - it addresses the engine's key weaknesses and comes with a 12-24 month warranty. Used units are cheaper but carry high risk without full documentation, particularly regarding turbocharger and VANOS condition. Rebuilds are justified for low‑mileage, high‑value examples (M760Li, Ghost) or where the owner plans long‑term preservation. Used: only with documented service history and proof of turbocharger maintenance. Reconditioned: best balance - all common weak points addressed, warranty included. Rebuilt: ideal for collector‑grade examples or long‑term keepers.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the N74B66 and the N74B66TU?

acceptedAnswer.text: The N74B66TU (Technical Update) is the version fitted to the BMW G11/G12 M760Li xDrive from 2016. It features revised cooling system components, different turbocharger mapping, and an xDrive‑specific oil pan and sump design to accommodate the all‑wheel‑drive system. Power output is 585-610 hp compared to 563-624 hp across the broader N74B66 family. The TU variant also benefits from improvements to the oil separation system and VANOS components. M760Li xDrive has the TU variant - it's not just a calibration difference. TU engines are not a direct swap into Rolls‑Royce applications without ECU and cooling changes. Verify your variant via the V5C or engine block stamp.

mainEntity.name: Is the N74B66 reliable, and what mileage can I expect?

acceptedAnswer.text: The N74B66 is one of BMW's most robust V12 designs, with an estimated lifespan of approximately 320,000 km (200,000 miles) when properly maintained. Many Rolls‑Royce and M760Li owners report 100,000+ trouble‑free miles with diligent maintenance. However, the engine is complex and expensive to maintain - turbocharger oil line coking, valve stem seal degradation and VANOS wear are real considerations on higher‑mileage examples. Budget for turbocharger oil line inspection and cleaning around 60,000 miles. Valve stem seal replacement should be considered around 80,000-100,000 miles. Full service history is essential - this is not an engine to neglect. The N74B66 is significantly more reliable than the naturally aspirated N73 it replaced.
